newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU eases pain for fishermen in quota deal.
newsitem.headline: EU eases pain for fishermen in quota deal.

text.p: The European Union agreed on Friday after gruelling all-night negotiations to soften proposed cuts in fish catch quotas in 1997, removing most of the pain for fishermen while protecting endangered stocks.
The European Commission, acting on scientific advice, had proposed further reductions aimed at safeguarding both run-down fish stocks and the future of the EU fishing industry.

"We have agreed sensible and pragmatic quotas," Irish Marine Minister Sean Barrett, who chaired the meeting, told a news conference after 21 hours of talks. "It was very exhausting and particularly complex."
EU Fisheries Commissioner Emma Bonino failed to appear at the news conference after collapsing at the end of the meeting, which also endorsed Norwegian and 10 other external fisheries agreements.
"The Commissioner was exhausted after two years of strenuous work without holidays. It finally caught up with her," said Commission fisheries spokesman Filippo di Robilant.
Di Robilant said that although ministers revised 30 out of the Commission's 116 quota proposals, the outcome was acceptable.
"We don't feel the Council overstepped the mark," di Robilant told the news conference.
But he warned that every year the margin for manoeuvre on fish quotas was being squeezed by declining stocks.
Belgium and Sweden voted against the quotas, officials said.
Belgium wanted a higher North Sea sole quota while Sweden wanted more cod under a compensation deal agreed when it joined the EU in 1995.
The Commission sought a 50 percent cut to 12,000 tonnes in catches of seriously depleted North Sea sole stocks but ministers raised this to 18,000. Belgium wanted 23,000 tonnes.
British Fisheries Minister Tony Baldry said he had won the best possible deal for British fishermen consistent with the need to protect stocks.
"The objectives that we set have all been achieved," Baldry told reporters after the meeting, citing an extra 21,000 tonnes of mackerel.
Northern Irish fishermen said they were pleased that the government had fulfilled a promise of extra fish, with their haddock quota doubled and an extra 2,000 tonnes of herring.
One of the most difficult issues was the allocation of quotas under new EU fisheries agreements with the Baltic States following Sweden and Finland's entry into the EU.
In the end there was unanimou agreements between the four countries concerned -- Germany, Denmark, Finland and Sweden.
Denmark reluctantly accepted the introduction of a 15,000-tonne quota for by-catches of herring by huge vessels hunting sprats for industrial processing into fish meal and oil.
Italy and Greece fought off quotas on tuna fishing in the Mediterranean, while measures to restrict sardine fishing off the coasts of Spain and Portugal were eased.
British fishermen gave the quotas deal a cautious welcome.
"It depends where you are fishing and for what," Barrie Deas, chief executive of Britain's National Federation of Fishermen's Organsiations, told Reuters.
There was good news for fishermen hunting haddock in the Irish Sea, angler fish off south west England and whiting off the west coast of Scotland, he said.
Scottish fishermen's leader Cecil Finn was more upbeat.
"It's much better than I expected," Finn told Reuters, noting that a proposed 25 percent cut in West of Scotland cod, haddock and whiting quotas had been pared to zero.
